Gender Imbalance in India: A Sociological Study of the Skewed Sex Ratio
abstract: Gender imbalance is a critical demographic concern that reflects the status of women and the nature of gender relations within society. India has istorically exhibited a skewed sex ratio unfavourable to females, shaped by deeply entrenchedsocio-cultural norms, economic structures, and institutional practices. This study provides a comprehensive sociological analysis of gender imbalance in India by examining trends in the sex ratio and its underlying determinants, including patriarchy, son preference, gender discrimination, and the misuse of reproductive technologies. Drawing on secondary data from the Census of India, the National Family Health Survey (NFHS), and existing scholarly literature, the study reveals that although the overall sex ratio has shown improvement in recent years, the sex ratio at birth continues to remain significantly imbalanced. This persistent disparity underscores the enduring influence of structural and cultural factors that perpetuate gender inequality. The study concludes that addressing gender imbalance requires not only effective policy implementation but also transformative changes in societal attitudes, gender norms, and power relations. Keywords:Sex ratio, gender inequality, patriarchy, female foeticide, India, sociological analysis

title: BRIDGING THE GAP IN GENDER DIVIDE: LAWS, DATA, MEDIA IMPACT AND SOCIETAL SHIFTS IN NATALITY INEQUALITY
abstract: his chapter examines the important topic of natality inequality in India, characterized by the imbalance in birth rates between male and female children. The desire for a male child, influenced by cultural, social, and economic practices, has resulted in a distorted sex ratio, due to variables like son preference, dowry customs, and patriarchal norms. This disparity has led to considerable societal repercussions, including an increase in aggression against women, human trafficking, and mental health challenges among men.

title: Production of desired livestock by sperm sorting technology : AReview
abstract: The objective of the study was to provide a review of sperm based sex selection/sorting in the livestock animals. The sperm sex selection play an important role in production of desirable sex animals. As in dairy industry need high mulching animals for continuing maintains of milk yield. Similarly in meat industry is also desire continuous supply of the male animals. Both above industry have high demand for their value added developed product in the market. Presently sperm sex selection technology available with us is very costly, required expert for handling equipment. It is patented technology hinder widespread application in the field. Several workers in the world have developed sperm sex selection methods. But none of the above is able to maintain repeatability and consistency in the sperm sex selection. Flow Cytometry technique is only commercial method till date. But, it further require lot of improvement in sorting efficiency, fertility ability and cost. In India sperm sex selection technology will solve many current problems and also achieve good animal production. In the future, it will fulfill the need of dairy and meat industry for supplying animal’s products to the raising population.

title: Essays on the Determinants of Human Capital
abstract: This dissertation consists of three empirical essays broadly concerned with the determinants of human capital. The first essay estimates the causal effect of exposure to maternal psychological stress generated by the 9/11 attacks on the cohort in utero that day. The analysis finds that cohorts exposed during the first or second trimester in New York City weighed less at birth and had shorter gestation lengths. Male and female newborns were affected similarly. At age six, boys were more likely to be in special education and more likely to be in kindergarten rather than first grade, with no effect on girls. Births outside New York City were not affected. The results suggest that psychological stress is an important channel through which adverse conditions experienced by pregnant women negatively impact the early life outcomes of in utero cohorts. The second essay (joint with Katherine Baldiga) presents experimental evidence of a gender difference in the valuation of job training as an explanation for the female advantage in human capital investment that has emerged in many high income countries. In an online labor market, we find that when subjects have limited experience with an unfamiliar task, women are more willing to pay for training than men, and women estimate that the returns to training are higher than men do. We find that task performance, the return to training, self-confidence, and risk aversion cannot explain the gender gap in valuing training. We present suggestive evidence that training may be valued by women for increasing their willingness to take on a challenge. The third essay tests the prediction of several biological theories that maternal condition impacts the sex ratio at birth and causes differential investment by child's sex with data from the Dominican Republic, a developing country with relatively neutral offspring sex preferences. The analysis finds that more educated women are more likely to give birth to sons, and women in the middle of the maternal age distribution are less likely to have a male child die during infancy. These results provide evidence that maternal condition is correlated with the sex composition of children.

title: Wahlberg, A. and Gammeltoft, T. (eds) Selective Reproduction in the 21st Century. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan. 2018. 198pp £72.00 (hbk) ISBN 978‐3‐319‐58219‐1.
abstract: Wahlberg and Gammeltoft's interest in the routinisation of reproductive technologies across the globe provided the basis for a prolific collaboration among scholars working in the area, resulting in the publication of Selective Reproduction in the 21st Century, a collection of ethnographic studies addressing the use of selective reproduction in different cultural, socio-economic and regulatory contexts. Defining selective reproduction as ‘practices that aim to prevent or promote the birth of particular kinds of children’ (p. 1), Wahlberg and Gammeltoft argue that the biomedical developments of the last 40 years, and the increasing availability of selective reproductive technologies (SRTs), ‘have separated reproduction from sex as well as genetics from gestation’ (p. 1). Rather than acting as a ‘helping hand’ as in the case of assisted reproduction, SRTs become a ‘guiding hand’, conceptualised as ‘a vote of no confidence against nature’ (p. 6). The collection is divided in three parts according to the purpose of selective reproduction: sex selection (chapters 2 and 3), prevention of disease and disability (chapters 4, 5, 6), and selection of traits (chapters 7 and 8). In chapter 2, Hang's ethnographic study of sex-selective abortions in Vietnam provides insight into the emotional experiences of 35 women before, during and after the abortion of female foetuses, a practice linked to cultural notions of son preference in this context. In chapter 3, Bhatia is concerned with what she terms ‘lifestyle sex selection’, that is, sex selection before pregnancy via preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and via MicroSort, a technique sorting sperm based on the chromosomes determining sex to be used with intrauterine insemination or IVF. Providing the historical framework within which these technologies developed in the United States and the United Kingdom, Bhatia analyses the interplay between scientific developments, politics, and ethics. In chapter 4, Heinsen engages with prenatal screening in Denmark, analysing the position of Danish pregnant women as ‘moral adherers’ of SRTs. Chapter 5 draws on Shih's research with Taiwanese women and couples, exploring the inextricable link between prenatal screening and testing and the cultural notion of ‘moral bearing’, and its translation as the prospective mothers’ responsibility to not bring a disabled child to society. Pavone and Lafuente Funes, in chapter 6, examine women's experiences of pre-implantation genetic diagnosis and pre-implantation genetic screening, across Spain, as a means to either overcome infertility or to avoid the transmission of hereditary disease. In chapter 7, Martin draws on her fieldwork in ‘fertility industry’ sites in the United States, where the use of third-party eggs is commercial, to illustrate how egg providers are recruited and managed as a marketing device for intending parents who desire children of specific racial-ethnic backgrounds or with particular physical and personality traits. In the last chapter of the collection, Stockey-Bridge explores the emotional investment of heterosexual and non-heterosexual Australian couples during the selection of egg donors and surrogates in the framework of commercial arrangements in India, and provides valuable insight into their decision-making processes. The collection makes a significant contribution to the growing literature of human reproduction in general and the interplay between reproduction, technology, and society in particular. The introduction provides a very useful overview of different SRTs and the important milestones that led to their development. Through the rich ethnographic accounts presented, the collection enhances our understanding of the accessibility of SRTs within diverse contexts, provides an in-depth look into the interpretations, decision-making, and the experiences of the people who engage with them, and generates thought-provoking questions on ethical considerations. In the Introduction, Wahlberg and Gammeltoft state that selective reproduction can be empirically examined through the technique(s) used (e.g. egg harvesting, sperm sorting, PGD, ultrasound screening, carrier testing), the sites where selective reproduction takes place (e.g. IVF clinics, prenatal care units, egg agencies), the people who engage with SRTs (prospective parents, practitioners and policy makers), as well as through the relevant legislation and guidelines. While the collection is indeed successful in bringing together the four empirical routes to the study of selective reproduction, the diversity of perspectives tackled could be argued to constitute the collection's major weakness. The reader becomes obliged to mentally ‘jump’ from women's (and generally users’) experiences to biomedical developments, and from laws and regulations to marketing strategies employed by commercial fertility hubs. In this respect, I found the book's structure somewhat challenging to follow. Nonetheless, the rich and complex insights of selective reproduction presented in the collection opens up new horizons for the understanding of contemporary selective reproduction practices around the world. A stimulating collection, Selective Reproduction in the 21st Century breaks new ground and leads to the development of further questions to be answered about current practices. Social scientists working in the areas of human reproduction, science and technology studies, health and illness, gender, and family and kinship studies, will find the book eye-opening.

title: Children and Maternal Migration: Evidence from Exogenous Variations in Family Size
abstract: Both theoretically and empirically, childbearing decreases labour supply of females, but few papers examine the effect of children on whether women emigrate to work. Using exogenous variations in family size induced by parents’ preferences for mixed sibling-sex composition in instrumental variable estimations, we find that, in Sri Lanka where most migrants are women and mothers, children decrease labour participation of females in the domestic market but they increase the likelihood of females working abroad.

title: Desire for male children -- an impediment to F.P. acceptance.
abstract: Although couples in rural and urban areas state an ideal number of children of 4 and 3 respectively, these number are very exceeded. A number of studies have shown the reason for this to be a desire for sons. The author examines the reasons for this, and finds the importance that is attached to sons imbedded deep in Indian culture. The importance of educating couples in the need for smaller families is underscored, and the author calls for a united effort to achieve this goal.

title: Trois essais sur les progrès de la santé et le développement économique en Afrique
abstract: This dissertation aims at opening the black box of African health progress during and followingthe colonial period. It does so by making three contributions to the literature on health policies,health standards and fertility patterns, in the 20th century’s Africa.The first chapter compares the colonial strategies for health policies’ provision and other colonialpolicies in former FrenchWest Africa between 1904 and 1958. Drawing on colonial archivesand existing data, it gathers a unique dataset containing colonial inputs at the colonial districtlevel: medical and educational staff, vaccinations, public work’s expenses and conscription.There was a very general strategy as regards to the provision of colonial services. In this context,the allocation of health inputs was specific in two dimensions only. First, medical staffwas used as a means of colonial “coverage”. Second, there is a long-lasting effect of preventionleading to a “diversification” strategy for all health investments. Away from these specificities,the common factors to all investments have to do with the colonial administration’s preferencefor path dependence, investments’ returns to scale, the diseases’ contagion risk and the demandfor colonial services. This work also suggests that there was no specialization of districtsin one type of investments.The second chapter of this thesis looks at the relationship between adult height and underfivemortality in the context of the “double African Paradox” in West Africa. Africans arerelatively tall in spite of extremely unfavorable income and disease environments. Moreover,their height stature decreased since the 1960’s despite improving health conditions and a fallin under-five mortality rates. This study points to selective mortality, by bringing forward apositive correlation between mothers’ height and mortality in the 1980’s West Africa. It thenestimates a new model of height differential between survivors and deceased. Results implythat selective mortality could be large enough to mask significant height increases in the 1980’sWest Africa. In high mortality contexts, anthropometric studies should discuss mortality levelsand trends. More generally, results imply that the issue of selective mortality is crucial to assessthe long-term impact of most health interventions.The third chapter tackles another specificity of African health: fertility and gender preferences.It develops a new indicator of gender preferences based on birth spacing. Applying it to Africaprovides evidence that son preference is strong and increasing in North Africa, whereas Sub-Saharan African countries display a preference for variety or no preference at all. Traditionalfamily systems accurately predict the nature of gender preferences, while religion does not.Last, the magnitude of preferences is stronger for wealthier and more educated women.

title: Urban Sex Ratio: A Study on Regional Wise Towns in Erstwhile Andhra Pradesh, India
abstract: Sex composition is an important aspect of the demographic structure. It is the result of a number of factors working together over a period. Imbalance is caused either by differential birth rate or differential death rate, which may be due to war or due to the custom of female infanticide or feticide. In addition to these, migration also causes significant difference in sex composition in a particular age group, which normally appears in the subsequent age group in due course of time. Imbalance in sex composition influences social, economic and community activities in a number of ways. Majority of one sex in the marriageable age group affects the marital life and later affects the natural growth rate. Males outnumbered in work force of the region in occupations such as mining and heavy industries where women cannot be absorbed. Variation in sex composition is a characteristic feature of towns. Sex composition differs greatly from suburbs and the rural areas due to the rural-urban migration and because of better medical facilities in the urban areas which has reduced mortality rates. Otherwise the sex variation at birth is same in rural and urban areas. Sex ratio is one such demographic factor which utters the development and intervenes of the technology directly or indirectly on men to women ratio. Insecurity among the women rose along with the developmental process and processes of urbanization. Hence the changing pattern of urban sex ration in the erstwhile Andhra Pradesh is studied with the help of the census data from 1961 to 2011.

title: Dimensions of population policy in India: the psycho-social implications.
abstract: All population policies, while seemingly identical in their formulation, differ in terms of their veritable ulterior objective. This is due to the fact that the formulation is done by a selected group of planning agencies and the health ministry. As the purport of the population policy rests more or less with the manipulation of the demographic variables, the important components of the population influencing policies should be discussed, as the population-influencing policies intend to impact on the population directly. The important components are fertility regulation, reductions in mortality and morbidity, and migration and population distribution. In India fertility regulations are directed toward achieving a reduced birth rate of 25 by 1984 or a growth rate of 1.25. While India has successfully reduced the mortality rate and the birth rate, the reduction in the rates are not proportional. This has led to a higher growth rate. Consequently, the pressure on the nation at this time is to reduce the birth rate. India has felt the strains of realizing this goal despite her concerted efforts for various reasons. First, birth control programs failed to gain as much acceptance as anticipated, whereas the plans designed to reduce mortality were moderately well received. Additionally, the birth control schemes came to have a cultural taboo, possibly attributable to inadequate and vague propaganda on the part of program administrators as well as illiteracy. Economic pro and con factors also contributed. The extent of migration in India is insignificant for various socioeconomic reasons. First, India is a country where illiteracy is predominant, and this has restrained the scope for migration. Secondly, as 80% of Indians depend on agriculture, they feel satisfied at home with whatever they earn. Regarding in-migration, India, as a developing country experiencing the ills of poverty, unemployment, low capital formation, and a slow pace of technological development, has not attracted in-migrants. India's efforts to delay the age at marriage either through law or persuasion have been futile as most of the young girls are neither in school nor gainfully employed. Laws governing inheritance should provide equal status for daughters whereby the preference to sons would undergo a change. Recently, India took a step in this direction by providing daughters with a share of their ancestral property, but this law gained little momentum in a society where daughters are deprived of any right over their ancestral or parental property. It appears that only a fraction of Indian women would welcome the provision of equal rights because nearly 80% of Indian women live in villages, which do not encourage a departure from the expected traditional role. When formulating population policy, attention should be given to its feasibility in the given social context.

title: Geology, Household Formation Rules and the Demand for Sons in Vietnam
[Demographic processes and the role of medical science and public health in improving the demographic composition].
abstract: Among the persons born in the RSFSR more than 1/2 are 1st born less than 1/3 are 2nd children and only about 1/10 are 3rd children or more. And since 10% of families are childless clearly the problem of the birthrate is serious in the RSFSR. In the countryside there is an increase in infant mortality and overall mortality and migrational patterns are changing the age and sex composition of the population. The increased resources put into health protection have not yielded the anticipated results. An effort must be made to single out the demographic features which can be influenced by state policy. The health of the population is one such factor and appropriate medical services can positively influence this.

title: A contractarian approach to the ethics of genetic-selective abortion
abstract: On March 24 of this year, Indiana Governor Mike Pence signed into law a bill1 banning abortions procured solely on account of a fetus's race, sex, or disability.2 In the last few years, North Dakota has similarly enacted a ban3 on abortions based on a fetus's gender or disability,4 Arizona has banned abortions ‘based on the sex or race’ of the fetus,5 and several other states have seen proposals for similar laws.6 As non-invasive prenatal genetic testing increases in ubiquity, it is likely that more such laws will be proposed and passed. This article is not an attempt to determine either the constitutionality of such laws7 or the feasibility of their actually being enforced. Instead this article concerns the prior moral issue raised by such proposals.8 If it were both constitutionally and practically possible to ban such abortions, would doing so be the morally fair choice? I will not treat this question as an issue of determining inalienable natural rights, nor of whether a fetus is a person, nor of other abstract moral questions. Nor will I approach the question from a strictly utilitarian position. Rather, I will frame the issue as a case where the interests of the present generation and future generations may conflict, and where we must reach a fair compromise between those generations. A paradigm example is John Rawls’ suggestion that a present generation surely has some responsibility to save and invest for the sake of future generations.9 This is the same sense of fairness that leads us to think that we ought to make some sacrifices today for the sake of preserving the environment for future generations.10 It may be less obvious that the reproductive decisions of today are similarly an intergenerational moral problem, but consider whether we would find it unfair if our generation decided to abort every pregnancy and become the last human generation, or decided to have sex-selective abortions that resulted in 75 per cent of the next generation being of the same sex and experiencing widespread romantic frustration.11 We would find these choices unfair in the same way that we would find choices that would destroy the environment after we are long dead to be unfair.12 The task, then, is to reach a rule of moral action that strikes the present generation (who necessarily make policy) as a fair compromise between its own and future generations. And the method I will use for striking that compromise is the same one that Rawls himself uses, the thought experiment of imagining ourselves behind a ‘Veil of Ignorance’, not knowing which generation we are going to be a part of, and from that ‘Original Position’ selecting the policy that we would find to be in our best interest.13 In Part I, I will lay out the picture of the original position that I think best serves the purpose of guiding our personal and policy choices on reproductive questions. Then, in Part II, I will apply that picture of the original position to the question of genetic-selective abortion by means of a thought experiment, considering both the possibility of a ban on all genetic-selective abortions and a narrower ban on only genetic-selective abortions based on traits that are not objectively debilitating. When contractarian moral philosophers have debated abortion ethics, the debate has generally boiled down to a disagreement over when we should imagine the original position choice to take place: at the moment of reaching enough maturity to actually understand one's desires, at the moment of birth, at the moment of conception, or (somehow) even prior to conception. This is essentially the same as to ask how much knowledge we should attribute to those behind the veil of ignorance—whether they should know, respectively, that they will reach maturity, that they will be born, that they will be conceived, or not even that they will be conceived. Scholars often treat this debate as a proxy war that inevitably determines the answer to the abortion question itself,14 and spend the bulk of their arguments on how to properly interpret the original position.15 An original position at birth almost automatically yields a pro-choice position, since one has no risk of being aborted,16 an original position at self-awareness leads to the same outcome with the possibility of even infanticide being permissible in some cases,17 while an original position at conception usually leads to a much more pro-life outcome.18 With so much riding on the question, how can we neutrally make the preliminary choice of when to imagine the original position occurring, without begging the question of the morality of abortion itself? The place to start is with the purpose of using the original position: it is a tool for us to make choices about our behavior as individuals and our governmental policy when those choices affect not just ourselves but others as well. An original position should be sensitive to every choice we can make that affects others, and also not sensitive to variables that are beyond our control. If a woman either voluntarily chooses to give birth to a fetus or is forced by the government to give birth to a fetus, this affects other people (the additional member of the population, and the people that he or she will interact with in his or her own life), and so a useful original position should be sensitive to the difference between giving birth and aborting. An original position at birth would miss the choice of whether to abort entirely, a choice that will affect other people, and so it cannot be complete.19 But an original position at conception also misses something, namely the choice (or government-compelled action) of whether to conceive at all. For exactly the same reason that not aborting affects future people, so does a choice or compulsion to conceive and then give birth also affect future people,20 and so an original position that is fully action-guiding must take this into account as well.21 Now we may seem to have a difficulty. If the original position ought to be before even conception, when is it? At the point of being a sperm, or an egg? In such a situation one's chances of actually being born would be so small that all choices regarding societal policy might seem meaningless, since they would concern a society one has almost no chance of joining.22 Again, however, we are saved by remembering that the original position should be sensitive only to changes in outcome that are affected by our choices. No matter what we choose to do, we cannot make every sperm or every egg into a born human being. As a high estimate we could say that the absolute maximum birth rate that could feasibly be achieved—either through individual choice or governmental coercion—would be 20 children per woman (roughly one birth for each year of fertility).23 An original position that imagined us as sperm, then, would be meaningless, because even in the extreme case each woman could only give birth to 20 of those sperm; the rest will go unborn no matter what choices we make.24 The original position in which we are one of the 20 people that a woman could, conceivably, give birth to is the one that is sensitive to all possible choices and not sensitive to the impossible, and thus is the correct one for an action-guiding rule of intergenerational fairness.25 So what are we in the original position I am proposing? We are not any physical entity like an infant, fetus, sperm, or egg. We might instead identify as something like ‘potential person born in [name of woman]'s [n]th year of fertility’, where ‘n’ is a number from 1 to 20. This is the picture of the original position that I propose should be used for analysing the fairness of reproductive policy to both present and future generations, and it is the one that I will use in this article.26 Genetic-selective abortions, when they are procured,27 are generally chosen by people in stable relationships who otherwise want to have children, and who can afford to undergo genetic testing before giving birth. In other words, they are likely, in the vast majority of cases, to be obtained by people who would try to ‘replace’ the aborted pregnancy with another conception later on.28 Hence, any increase in the overall odds of being born by banning this particular type of abortion (as opposed, for example, to a ban on abortions in accidental unmarried pregnancies) would likely be negligible. Does this mean that someone in the original position would have no interest in banning genetic-selective abortions? Not necessarily, because someone in the original position might care not just about his odds of being born, but also about his expected quality of life if he is born, and the reason for not having a life if he is not born. To fully weigh the costs and benefits to both the present generation and future generations from such a ban, and to get a sense of the choice we ourselves would make in the original position, we can imagine a thought experiment that would present us with an analogous choice. Suppose you and 19 other people have contracted a rare and, if untreated, fatal disease and are soon to fall into a coma. The antidote will not be ready until after the coma has set in. Even worse, only two doses will be ready before the disease progresses to the point of death. Only two people will be saved; the other 18 will die in their comas, never feeling pain and never knowing that the medicine was chosen not to be given to them. Now, before the coma sets in, the group must choose which decision method it wants the hospital to use in deciding which two people to give the antidote to. The first method is complete randomness, a draw of two numbers from a hat containing 20 numbers after you have entered the coma. The second method is to do a genetic test on each of you after you have entered the coma (at this point, you are all the same age, and none have yet undergone such a genetic test, and so no one has any information as to how they would fare on this test relative to anyone else). This test would be only for serious latent genetic diseases that would manifest later in life, and that would seriously diminish either the quality or length of life, or both.29 Anyone with such a latent disease would be disqualified, and two people would be randomly chosen to receive the antidote from the remainder who are not disqualified. The third method is to undergo a more rigorous genetic test. This would not just look at objective markers of quality of life, but also more subjective qualities—likelihood of criminality or antisociability, particularly remarkable capacity for talents in fields such as math or music, capacity for diligence or charity, etc. After a holistic review taking into account both objective quality of life standards and more subjective qualities, with an eye both to likelihood of happiness and likelihood of being a boon to society as a whole, a panel of experts would pick the two to be given the antidote. Once again, no one in the group has undergone such a genetic test, and no one has an ability to guess how they will do relative to the others. As a side effect of the antidote, your future offspring (whether you are male or female) can only be genetically tested in the womb to the same extent that you were tested prior to taking the antidote. And so if you choose the first method and survive, you will not be able to perform any genetic tests on your future offspring (and thus not obtain any information on which to obtain an abortion). If you choose the second method and survive, you will be able to test your future offspring for objective but not subjective genetic traits (and likewise, obtain an abortion based on the former information but not the latter). Finally, if you choose the third method and survive, you will be able to test your future offspring for both objective and subjective genetic traits, and choose whether to obtain an abortion based on the totality of that knowledge. You are about to go into the coma, and the other 19 have elected you to choose the method of selection that will be used on the whole group. Which of the three would you, reader, choose? The first method, randomness, corresponds to choosing a complete ban on taking genetics into account in obtaining an abortion in the original position. A couple has two children; which two people are born is simply a matter of which two fall into the first two ‘slots’ in the birth order. Even if a test would show that they are the two most likely to have a serious genetic defect and a seriously diminished quality of life, they would be born anyway, because the results of that test could not be used as the reason to abort them and conceive again. The second method, objective characteristics, corresponds to a law allowing prospective parents to obtain an abortion taking into account serious birth defects or other major obstacles to quality of life, as indicated by genetic testing, but not more subjective tests such as personality or aptitude measures (and not physical characteristics that are in no way a disability, such as race or gender).30 The third method, the holistic review, corresponds to a law allowing abortions for all reasons that can be learned from genetic testing, and would allow parents to reject the genetic makeup of a conceived fetus and obtain an abortion in the hopes of conceiving one with a more desirable genetic profile. The first thing to notice in evaluating these options is that if chance of survival were all that an individual in this position cared about, she would be completely ambivalent about which of the three methods to choose. Since she would have no information about how she would perform on the genetic tests relative to the other 19 people, the test would be functionally just as random as the drawing of numbers from a hat. With present knowledge, her odds of waking up from the coma, no matter which method of decision is used, are 10 per cent. The second method, however, increases the expected quality of life of the two survivors compared to the first method, because the fact that they awaken from the coma would guarantee that they have no serious latent genetic disorders. Thus, it effectively increases the expected utility of those in the position of choosing a method without in any way increasing their odds of dying.31 In addition to this comparative benefit, the second method also grants someone the ability to avoid raising someone with serious and potentially life-consuming disabilities in the future, should they choose to obtain a prenatal genetic test.32 The third method is more troubling, in that it allows others to make a judgement of worth based on intrinsic characteristics over which a person has no control, a judgement that will not necessarily be motivated by choosing people who will experience the highest utility. Consider the recent case of a mother who sued a sperm bank after finding that the sperm she was artificially inseminated with came from an African-American.33 Suppose she had used genetic testing before giving birth to discover this fact, and based on this knowledge had decided to obtain an abortion. There is no doubt we would at least find this morally troubling; it seems to be deciding the fate of a future person based on his future skin color. Similarly, we would be troubled if the panel, say, chose one of the 20 to not receive the antidote because that person was gay, or a racial minority, or female. Even when a choice is made based on genetic characteristics such as ‘sociability’ that may be relevant to the rest of society, we could still imagine that this would be an insulting cause of one's death. Crucially, even though I would never know that this is the reason I didn't wake up (just as the aborted fetus would never know he or she was aborted because of his or her genetic profile) it would gall me now, before I fall into the coma, if I knew that that was a possibility. This, I think, is the same attitude we would take in the original position. And it presents a justification for drawing the line at objectively debilitating, but not subjectively disfavored, genetic characteristics as legitimate reasons for abortion. The main benefit of choosing the third method would be the increased utility to all from a world in which many of the people they interact with were chosen after such a holistic review, but just how much of a positive effect this would have on society is doubtful, since it is not clear that many parents, even if legally allowed to, would engage in such selection. Further, unlike the freedom to escape the burden of raising children with objectively debilitating conditions, the benefit of the freedom to not introduce into society a child that is less than optimal seems slim. For these reasons, I would find the risks of the third method to outweigh the potential benefits, and I would choose the second method. We must consider, however, an important aspect in which this thought experiment is not identical to the pre-conception original position. Although 18 people going into the coma will never have a moment of realization that they were not chosen because they did not pass the genetic test, they are aware beforehand that such a risk exists. This is different from the experience of the actual aborted fetus. It has never had the capability to understand the concepts of genetics, abortion, or even the fact that other creatures exist in the world. Should we say that a creature in such a state ought not to be considered ‘harmed’ by choices that implicate its dignity in the same way that a person who understands such concepts might be harmed? I don't think so, because it is possible to inflict harms that a person not only is never aware has happened, but never even contemplated could have happened (for example, spitting in a person's food, or dumping them in an unmarked grave after they are dead). Even in the case of facts that we ‘don't know we don't know about’, we can say that they are still harms, because people have an implied preference for things to happen that they would have preferred if they had understood and been made explicitly aware of the possibility.34 Undeniably, this presents a difficulty for putting such questions in the of a thought experiment to test our own because putting the decision in the of would you the thought experiment in such a way that you have a choice. this choice you to know of the beforehand and know what might potentially This is not Now that you have given your answer to the thought experiment as we can the thought experiment so that you fall into a coma before even knowing you have the Now, the choice is to be made by a not this to have happened, are you, reader, ambivalent about what the It seems to me that you would the chooses you would have chosen in the when you had knowledge and were given a choice.
